Fast reliable pricing and calibration of the rough Heston model IIThanks:  S.B.: Department of Economics, The University of Texas at Austin, 2225 Speedway Stop C3100, Austin, TX 78712–0301, sboyarch@utexas.edu
M.I.: Deutsche Bank, 21 Moorfields, London, EC2Y 9DB. Email address: marcdein@gmail.com
S.L.: Calico Science Consulting. Austin, TX. Email address: levendorskii@gmail.com

Svetlana Boyarchenko, Marco de Innocentis and Sergei Levendorskiĭ
Abstract.

This is an extended and modified version of the preprint “Fast reliable pricing and calibration of the rough Heston model ”. We suggest new fast and accurate methods for pricing and calibration of the rough Heston model and analyze relative advantages of several popular methods of numerical Fourier inversion. The pricing method and analysis of other methods are quite general and applicable to wide classes of models where the characteristic functions can be calculated explicitly or numerically. In application to the rough Heston model, it is necessary to numerically solve the fractional Volterra equation. We analyze sources of errors of several variations of the Adams method, and construct a modification that increases accuracy of the solution. For moderate or long maturities and strikes near spot, thousands of prices are computed in several milliseconds (ms) in Matlab on a Mac with moderate specs, with relative errors ≲10−4\lesssim 10^{-4}. Even for options close to expiry and far-OTM, the pricing takes a few tens or hundreds of ms.

We show that, for the calibrated parameters in El Euch and Rosenbaum (Math. Finance 2019, v. 29), the model implied vol surface is much flatter and fits the market data poorly; thus the calibration in op. cit. is a case of “ghost calibration” (M. Boyarchenko and S. Levendorskiĭ, Quant. Finance 2015, v. 15): the numerical error and model specification error offset each other, creating an apparently good fit that vanishes when a more accurate pricer is used. We explain how such errors arise in popular iFT implementations that use fixed numerical parameters, yielding spurious smiles/skews, and provide numerical evidence that SINH acceleration (S. Boyarchenko and S. Levendorskiĭ IJTAF 2019, v. 22), of Fourier inversion is faster and more accurate than competing methods. Robust error control is ensured by a general Conformal Bootstrap principle that we formulate; the principle is applicable to many Fourier-pricing methods. We outline how this principle and our method enable accurate calibration procedures that are hundreds of times faster than approaches commonly used in the industry. Using the methods developed in the paper and the CB principle, we address the outstanding problem Markovian or non Markovian - which class of models fits the empirical data best.

Disclaimer: The views expressed herein are those of the authors only. No other representation should be attributed.

Key words: rough Heston model, fractional Adams method, Fourier transform, sinh-acceleration, CM method, COS method, Lewis method, calibration, conformal bootstrapping principle

1. Introduction

Pricing methods based on the Fourier transform are amenable to fast calculations, hence, widely used for calibration of various models. However, pricing errors can have serious impact on calibration results and an assessment of the relative performance of models. As demonstrated in [11], naive applications of popular Fourier methods with fixed, non-optimal parameters can lead to ghost calibration. In this phenomenon, numerical inaccuracies of the pricing algorithm systematically offset the model’s specification errors, producing a fallacious, yet seemingly excellent, fit to market data with incorrect model parameters and a distorted implied volatility surface. Conversely, the correct model may be ruled out simply because, at the true parameters, numerical error dominates: sundial calibration [53]: a sundial never shows midnight. The first aim of the paper is to analyze sources of errors of several popular methods of Fourier inversion, and compare their performance in application to the Heston model and rough Heston model. The analysis admits a straightforward modification to the Bates model and its rough analog, and, if errors of numerical evaluation of the characteristic function are properly taken into account, to more complicated stochastic volatility (SV) models and models with stochastic interest rates. In the case of the Heston model, Bates model and other simple models, the characteristic function is calculated explicitly. If certain complex-analytical subtleties are properly taken into account, a careful choice of an algorithm for the Fourier inversion guarantees that the option price is calculated sufficiently accurately. If the characteristic function can be calculated only numerically, then an additional source of errors appears, and the errors increase as the maximal absolute value of the spectral parameter ξ\xi that is used in the quadrature for the Fourier inversion increases. Let NN be the number of terms in the numerical procedure for the Fourier inversion, and MM the number of time steps in a chosen quadrature for the evaluation of the characteristic function. Then, typically, MM necessary to satisfy a given error tolerance increases with NN, and, for small times to maturity, NN must be large; hence, for small maturities, both MM and NN must be large, and accurate option pricing becomes very time consuming. If time to maturity TT is large and a relatively simple quadrature for the evaluation of the characteristic function is used, then MM must be large as well. Only for moderate maturities, and for strikes KK not far from the spot, moderately large NN and MM can be used in essentially any reasonable procedure. In other regions of the maturity-strike space, an accurate pricing procedure is difficult to design. Following Leo Tolstoy (“All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way”), we formulate the Anna Karenina principle for option pricing: in a good region of the (K,T)(K,T)-space, all reasonable models and pricing methods are alike; close/far from maturity and far in the tails, models and pricing methods perform differently11 1 Disclaimer: we are not the first to formulate the principle. J. Diamond [31] formulated the principle in applications to biology: “A deficiency in any one of a great number of factors can render a species undomesticable. Therefore, all successfully domesticated species are not so because of a particular positive trait, but because of a lack of any number of possible negative traits.” . Even if the pricer is sound, in applications, the restrictions on the CPU cost imply that one cannot choose both NN and MM very large. One is tempted to use the same parameters of the numerical scheme for all (K,T)(K,T) in the data set and all parameters of the model. Hence, typically, too small NN and/or MM are used, and the error depends on the choice. If NN is small, the error of the numerical Fourier inversion is large; if NN is large but MM is insufficiently large, then the characteristic function is evaluated with large errors; the relative errors can be of the order of thousands percent and more. We formulate the Uncertainty Principle of calibration: using different parameters of the numerical scheme, one can produce a host of different prices and volatility curves and surfaces, and choose shapes one likes better.

In the paper, we demonstrate these effects in the case of the rough Heston model [36]. We suggest new fast and accurate methods for pricing and calibration of the rough Heston model and analyze errors of several popular methods of numerical Fourier inversion, which lead to the ghost and sundial calibration. The pricing method and analysis of other methods are quite general and applicable to wide classes of models where the characteristic functions can be calculated explicitly or numerically. In particular, modifications of pricing and calibration procedures constructed in the paper can be easily adjusted to generalizations of the rough Heston model of Bates type. In application to the rough Heston model, it is necessary to numerically solve the fractional Volterra equation. We suggest modifications that increase accuracy of the solution. As it is explained in [54], even in classical affine models, accurate numerical solution of a system of Riccati equations can be difficult and serious errors can result. In the numerical example for the two-factor CIR model considered in [54], a numerically calculated trajectory for the cumulant ϕ⁡(T,ξ)\phi(T,\xi), with a fairly small time step, blows up as T→∞T\to\infty although according to the theoretical analysis, the exactly calculated trajectory does not blow up. In the case of the fractional Volterra equation, the theoretical results available in the mathematical literature are very far from being complete, in the case of large (in absolute value) spectral parameter ξ\xi especially. For design of accurate numerical schemes, the following difficulties must be taken into account; similar difficulties arise for other models but the detailed analysis is model-specific. Let time to maturity TT be fixed. For accurate Fourier inversion, ϕ⁡(T,ξ)\phi(T,\xi) with large ξ\xi must be used and the number of terms NN in the chosen quadrature must be large; for large ξ\xi, very large number of time steps MM is necessary to calculate ϕ⁡(T,ξ)\phi(T,\xi) sufficiently accurately. We consider in detail several variations of the Adams method in applications to the fractional Volterra equation. The inherent instability of numerical solutions of the latter leads to the following interesting effect. Let TT and MM be fixed, and MM is insufficiently large. Then, if one variation of the Adams method is used, Re⁡ϕ⁡(T,ξ)\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(T,\xi) may start to increase as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty along the line of integration. Hence, the pricing error becomes too large if large ξ\xi are used, and the calculated price falls outside the no-arbitrage bounds. If another variation of the Adams method is used, Re⁡ϕ⁡(T,ξ)→−∞\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(T,\xi)\to-\infty, and very fast. Then the sequence of prices evaluated using longer ξ\xi grids converges extremely fast, and one is tempted to conclude that the convergence of the method is excellent - although the reason is that all additional terms become irrelevant. The excellent convergence is fallacious, and the residual non-negligible error remains. The residual error depends on the parameters of the model, maturity and strike, and can be rather large. To control the errors in difficult situations where the theoretically sound error control is unavailable or too complicated for practical purposes, we suggest the Conformal Bootstrap principle (CB principle). We use the principle in applications to the Heston and rough Heston models; the principle can be used in applications to other models as well. The main idea is to use different conformal deformations of the contour of integration in the pricing formula, make the corresponding conformal changes of variables and apply a good quadrature to the resulting integral over ℝ{\mathbb{R}} or ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}. If the prices obtained with different deformations agree up to the error 10−m10^{-m}, where m≥5m\geq 5, we surmise that each of the prices differ from the one calculated with a perfect pricer by not more than 10−m+210^{-m+2}. If a simply connected region of analyticity of the characteristic function where the initial contour and deformed one lie are known and the leading term of asymptotics of the cumulant at infinity is known as well, then admissible deformations are known. Furthermore, for each deformation, sufficiently accurate prescriptions for the step ζ\zeta and number of terms NN of the simplified trapezoid rule are easy to derive. The prescription being an approximate one, small adjustments by 10% - 30% may be needed; in some cases, up to 80%. The CB principle allows one to essentially guarantee that the pricing formula with the chosen ζ\zeta and NN produces prices with the desired accuracy. We discuss the reliability of the ad-hoc CB principle in the case when the domain of the analyticity of the integrand in the pricing formula is unknown.

In the first version of the paper, as an efficient family of deformations, we used the sinh-deformation defined by conformal maps of the form ξ=i​ω1+b​sinh⁡(i​ω+y)\xi=i\omega_{1}+b\sinh(i\omega+y) and the simplified trapezoid rule. In addition to the sinh-family of deformations, we also used (in different publications), the fractional-polynomial deformations and logarithmic deformations of ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, and, in applications to evaluation of probability distributions of stable Lévy processes, deformations of ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}. In the case of integrals over ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}, the most efficient family is the rotation of ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}. After the rotation, we apply the exponential change of variable and simplified trapezoid rule. The families of deformations of ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+} are sufficiently flexible for efficient evaluation of distributions and pricing options if the characteristic function admits a bound via exp⁡(−c​|ξ|ν)\exp(-c|\xi|^{\nu}), where ν∈(0,2)\nu\in(0,2), in the union of a strip and cone around the line of integration in the Fourier inversion formula. The families work well even if ν∈(0,1)\nu\in(0,1), hence, the characteristic function decays slowly at infinity. In the present paper, we introduce an alternative to the sinh-acceleration, the rotation of the contour of integration ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+} in the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature (GL quadrature). Assume that the integrand can be evaluated very accurately at a small CPU cost and the error tolerance is not smaller than E-10, which is sufficient for any practical application. We prove that if the sinh-deformation (or rotation of ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}_{+}) is applicable and either ν>1\nu>1 or ν=1\nu=1 and c>1c>1, then the efficiency of the rotated GL quadrature is comparable to the sinh-acceleration but the number of terms in the GL quadrature is 20-50% larger. If ν<1\nu<1 or ν=1\nu=1 and c<1c<1, then the theoretical error bound for the GL quadrature gives +∞+\infty. If f⁡(y)f(y) is the integrand, the error bound is in terms of high order derivative of f0​(y)=ey​f​(y)f_{0}(y)=e^{y}f(y). Hence, one expects that increasing number of terms, one obtains a diverging sequence. Surprisingly, we observed that, for moderately large number of terms, the GL quadrature works well if ν=1\nu=1 and c<1c<1 (which is the case for all parameter sets of the Heston model and rough Heston models that we considered if time to maturity TT is not rather large) but cc is not too close to 0. Apparently, in cases when the GL quadrature is surprisingly accurate, there exists a sufficiently accurate approximation of the integrand by a function which decays at infinity faster than e−|ξ|e^{-|\xi|} but insignificantly differs from the characteristic function on the interval that contains all nodes of the GL quadrature with a chosen number of terms NN. However, relatively simple error bounds that we managed to derive using this interpretation imply significantly larger errors than we observe.

Thus, one can try to use the rotated GL quadrature instead of the sinh-acceleration but the results will be not reliable, for short maturity options especially unless high precision arithmetic is used. In the case of Heston model and rough Heston model, c=c⁡(T)→0c=c(T)\to 0 as T→0T\to 0; heuristically, we hope that if the results produced for 2-3 different rotations agree well, then the prices are sufficiently accurate, as in the case when the sinh-acceleration is applied. This conclusion can be false if the fallacious variation of the Adams method is used. In this case several dozens of non-neglible terms in the GL quadrature applied after different rotations are values of the same analytic functions. Hence, the difference of the price calculated using an ideal pricer and the sums of the non-negligible terms in the simplified trapezoid rule must be identical (up to the machine error).

Using the methods developed in the paper and the CB principle, we address the outstanding problem Markovian or non Markovian - which class of models fits the empirical data best. Starting with the celebrated Heston model [47], affine models have become one of the most popular classes of stochastic volatility models, term structure models, and models in FX. The popularity is due to the fact that the characteristic function in an affine model can be explicitly calculated solving an associated system of generalized Riccati equations [33], hence, the Fourier transform technique allows one to express prices of options of the European type as oscillatory integrals. However, despite their analytical convenience, models based on classical affine diffusions such as Heston have well-documented limitations in reproducing key features of observed implied volatility surfaces. In particular, these models are unable to capture adequately the pronounced short-maturity steepness of implied volatility smiles – a feature consistently observed in equity and FX markets. In response to these shortcomings, a new class of models, that of rough volatility models, has been proposed. These models replace the standard Brownian Motion (BM) drivers of volatility with fractional processes characterised by a Hurst index H∈(0,1/2)H\in(0,1/2). Empirical evidence presented by Gatheral, Jaisson, and Rosenbaum [44] demonstrated that, at the time, the log-volatility of financial assets behaved as a fractional Brownian motion with H≈0.1H\approx 0.1, both in historical and implied volatility data. This low Hurst index implies a “rough” volatility path that is far less smooth than Brownian motion, leading to stronger short-term memory and more accurate modelling of the volatility clustering and bursts which are often observed in financial markets. For various aspects of rough volatility models, see [8, 44, 51, 36, 40, 39, 41, 42, 9] and the bibliographies therein.

By the law of the pendulum, several recent empirical publications (see, e.g., [46, 49] and the bibliographies therein) cast doubts on the superiority of rough volatility models as compared to Markovian ones. The following main shortcomings are formulated: the volatility skew is too high at the short end and too low at the long end as compared to the skew inferred from the market data, the log-log plot of ATM skew is a downward sloping straight line although the corresponding curve inferred from the market data is concave, and the implied volatility surfaces in rough volatility models agree poorly with the market ones. In the paper, we include a preliminary analysis of these conclusions. A detailed analysis requires a systematic empirical study which is outside the scope of the paper. In several examples of implied volatility curves calculated for the rough Heston model, which we found in the literature, the errors are of the order of several percent or more, hence, the calculated model surfaces are far from the correct ones. Thus, the claim that the surfaces in rough Heston models fit the market ones very poorly can be attributed to inaccuracy of the numerical methods used. If the pricing method is sufficiently accurate, the model surface can be fairly close to the market one, even in a fairly difficult situation. In the present paper, we calibrate the rough Heston model to the implied volatility surface of TSLA on 2 May, 202522 2 Tesla (TSLA) was among the most actively traded option underlyings in 2025, which makes it a natural test case.. The trading activity was hectic on this day, which makes the example interesting from the point of view of applications to the risk management, and the calibrated data set enjoys (rather, suffer) difficult properties for any two-factor model to fit well. (We discuss non-typical properties this set of data below.) Nevertheless, the model surface is fairly close to the market one (see Fig. 1 and implied volatility curves in Sect. 7.1).

If the model implied volatilities differ from the market ones by several percent or more, the accuracy of the numerical calculation of the derivative of the implied volatility w.r.t. strike becomes very poor indeed. In many cases, if a more accurate pricing method is used, the shapes of the implied volatility surfaces, curves, and skews significantly change. For instance, in the numerical example in [36], the ATM skew at the short end drops by more than 100% when we recalculate the skew using more accurate methods. We calculated the ATM skews for the sets of parameters used in the paper and several other sets; in all cases, the log-log ATM skew is concave up starting from maturities 1-3 days (depending on model’s parameters). In the case of TSLA, 2 May, 2025, the concavity is small.

In our numerical experiments, we observed that as the accuracy of the pricing procedure improves, the skew becomes significantly lower at the short end and may become higher at the long end. Sufficiently accurate calculations for the interval 1D-1W require M=40000M=40000 even if the new efficient modification of the Adams method is used. We suspect that all numerical results that can be found in the literature are obtained with less accurate numerical schemes and time steps are larger than necessary. For instance, in [60], M=200M=200 is mentioned, in other texts, M=2000M=2000 is used. We found that to obtain good calibration results for the data set used in the present paper, even M=4000M=4000 is too small if one wishes to obtain sufficiently accurate results. Hence, the calculated curves and surfaces that can be found in the literature are incorrect and correctly calculated ones can fit the market ones significantly better. The analysis of the sources of errors at the short end is one of the main objectives of the paper.33 3 To conduct a satisfactory analysis at the long end, where the errors of numerical solution of the fractional Adams equation accumulate, it is necessary to use hybrid methods with more efficient methods applied outside a small neighborhood of 0. We leave this natural extension of the paper to the future. It is possible that the agreement of the model skew with the market one will improve in the region of long maturities as well.

We were unable to find examples in the literature where very fine grids were used, hence, the common belief about the shape of the log-log ATM skew in the rough Heston model is based not on reliable calculations of model skews but on the asymptotic result in [43]. But an asymptotic formula cannot be expected to give a good approximation outside a small neighborhood of zero. An additional problem is that the observed implied volatility curves are just several dots - for short maturities, about a dozen or less. Hence, the market skew is not even a well-defined object. If we define the market skew using finite differences (as in [43]), then, typically, the result strongly depends on the choice of the finite difference and the difference among different market skews blows up as T→0T\to 0. To make a meaningful comparison of the market and model skews, it is necessary to know how the market skew is calculated and apply the same approximate procedure to the model. Typically, at the short end, the accurately calculated derivative differs significantly from each finite difference. An example using the real data TSLA on 2 May, 2025, obtained on a hectic date of the financial shows an unexpectedly good performance of the rough Heston model. The rough Heston model gives excellent fit even when extrapolated across expiries. The out-of-sample performance of the Heston model is significantly worse. We have chosen the date for calibration as an important one from the point of view of applications in risk management. Later, we observed the following interesting atypical feature of this empirical parameter set: in a sizable neighborhood of the spot, the implied volatility curve is close to a segment of the downward sloping straight line. See Fig. 2, where we compare 1W curves for Apple, AMD and Amazon on 8 Aug, 2025, and the leading example TSLA on 2 May, 2025. The tails are steeper, especially the left one (see Fig.  2). A shape of this kind can be reproduced in a one-factor model with a reasonably small AVE as we demonstrate; but then the ATM skew significantly differs from the market one. The example of TSLA on 2 May, 2025, seems to be an outlier. We leave to the future a study of models which can reproduce the implied volatility curves with an approximately straight segment around the ATM strike. Probably, one-factor models are incapable of producing a small AVE and the ATM skew which is close to the market one. In other respects, the rough Heston model performs in this case very well. The detailed analysis of the out-of-sample performance is in Sect. 7.

A further motivation for rough volatility models comes from counterparty credit risk. One of us implemented the Heston model for risk-factor evolution and pricing within the counterparty credit risk (CCR) engine of a major bank, a setting in which the use of a stochastic volatility model had until a few years earlier seemed impractical, but became necessary for realistic exposures. The extreme volatility clustering seen in recent episodes of market stress suggests that rough volatility models may, in time, play a similar role in CCR and CVA, as well as in stress testing. This however requires pricing to be fast and reliable enough for the millions of revaluations such applications demand, which is the use case our method targets.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The rough Heston model and several methods of the solution of the fractional Volterra equations are introduced in Sect. 2. In Sect. 3, we recall the Flat iFT and SINH-acceleration methods, give explicit recommendations for the choice of the parameters of the SINH-acceleration, and consider the Conformal Bootstrap principle. In Sect. 4, we analyze several popular methods of the Fourier inversion. In particular, we outline the rotated version of the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature and a version of the Conformal Bootstrap principle based on the the rotated version. Numerical examples are in Sect. 5. Pricing algorithms and calibration results are in Sect.6- 7. Sect.  8 concludes. The detailed pricing/calibration algorithms and additional tables and figures are in the appendix.

2. Rough Heston model and the fractional Volterra equation

2.1. Formulas for the characteristic function

The rough Heston model [36] is constructed by replacing the variance process in the Heston model with the fractional square root process:

(2.1) d​St\displaystyle dS_{t} =\displaystyle= St​Vt​d​Bt,\displaystyle S_{t}\sqrt{V_{t}}dB_{t},
(2.2) Vt\displaystyle V_{t} =\displaystyle= V0+1Γ⁡(H+1/2)​∫0t(t−s)H−1/2​(γ⁡(θ−Vs)​𝑑s+γ​ν​Vt​d​Ws),\displaystyle V_{0}+\frac{1}{\Gamma(H+1/2)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{H-1/2}(\gamma(\theta-V_{s})ds+\gamma\nu\sqrt{V_{t}}dW_{s}),

where S0,V0>0S_{0},V_{0}>0 and (Bt,Wt)(B_{t},W_{t}) is BM in 2D with the correlation coefficient ρ∈[−1,1]\rho\in[-1,1]; the components are standard BM in 1D. Proof.

It suffices to note that I1−α​Iα=I1I^{1-\alpha}I^{\alpha}=I^{1}. ∎

2.2. Asymptotics of ϕ⁡(ξ,τ):=g1​(ξ,τ)+v​g2​(ξ,τ)\phi(\xi,\tau):=g_{1}(\xi,\tau)+vg_{2}(\xi,\tau) as τ→∞\tau\to\infty

The asymptotic formula is an analog of the formula rigorously derived in [53] in the Heston model. Unfortunately, we were unable to rigorously prove the formula in the case of the rough Heston model and the validity of the assumption that ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)\phi(\xi,\tau) admits analytic continuation to an open cone 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} containing (0,+∞)(0,+\infty). We verified the latter property for a number of sets of the parameters of the model using the conformal bootstrap principle. The second assumption that we make is that as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty remaining in 𝒞{\mathcal{C}},

(2.11) h⁡(ξ,τ)=h∞​ξ+O⁡(1),h(\xi,\tau)=h_{\infty}\xi+O(1),

where h∞∈ℂ∖{0}h_{\infty}\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{0\}. We also empirically verified this assumption in a number of examples. Substituting (2.11) into (2.9), dividing by ξ\xi and passing to the limit ξ→∞\xi\to\infty, we observe that (2.11) fails unless h∞h_{\infty} is a solution of the equation

Now we can calculate the asymptotics of ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)\phi(\xi,\tau):

where

and v0:=V0v_{0}:=V_{0}. Note that if α=1\alpha=1, then the asymptotic formula (2.13) coincides with the formula for the Heston model derived in [53]. We observed that numerically calculated ϕ\phi satisfies ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)/ξ→c∞​(τ)\phi(\xi,\tau)/\xi\to c_{\infty}(\tau) with a good accuracy. See Fig. 3.

However, for large |ξ||\xi|, the difference ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)−c∞​(τ)​ξ\phi(\xi,\tau)-c_{\infty}(\tau)\xi can be large, and the sign of Re⁡(ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)−c∞​(τ)​ξ)\operatorname{\rm Re}(\phi(\xi,\tau)-c_{\infty}(\tau)\xi) can strongly depend on a numerical scheme chosen to evaluate ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)\phi(\xi,\tau).

2.3. Ad hoc recommendation for the choice of the cone of analyticity

The choice of the cone 𝒞γ−,γ+{\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}} is necessary to give a recommendation for the choice of the crucial parameters ω\omega and dd, and then ζ\zeta and Λ\Lambda of the SINH-acceleration method. We set c∞r​e​(τ)=Re⁡c∞​(τ)c^{re}_{\infty}(\tau)=\operatorname{\rm Re}c_{\infty}(\tau), c∞i​m​(τ)=c∞​(τ)c^{im}_{\infty}(\tau)=c_{\infty}(\tau), and find 𝒞γ−,γ+{\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}} as a cone such that for any ray ei​γ​ℝ+⊂𝒞γ−,γ+e^{i\gamma}{\mathbb{R}}_{+}\subset{\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}}, the real part of −[i​ξ​ln⁡K+i​c∞i​m​(τ)+c∞r​e​(τ)]​ei​γ-[i\xi\ln K+ic^{im}_{\infty}(\tau)+c^{re}_{\infty}(\tau)]e^{i\gamma} is positive. and approximately optimal recommendation for the choice of ω,d\omega,d are as follows.

2.4. Fractional Adams method and its modifications

2.4.1. Adams method

One fixes a uniform grid (tj)j∈ℤ+(t_{j})_{j\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}, tj=j​Δt_{j}=j\Delta, and calculates the approximations h^​(ξ,tk),k=1,2,…,\hat{h}(\xi,t_{k}),k=1,2,\ldots, in two steps. First, the predictor h^P​(ξ,tk),k=1,2,…,\hat{h}^{P}(\xi,t_{k}),k=1,2,\ldots, is calculated, and then the more accurate approximation h^​(ξ,tk),k=1,2,….\hat{h}(\xi,t_{k}),k=1,2,\ldots. To calculate the former, the rectangular rule is used while the latter is evaluated using the trapezoid rule. At the first steps, in the region of large |ξ||\xi| and small tjt_{j}, significant errors appear. The errors are especially clearly seen at the first step of the induction procedure, which we write explicitly:

(2.15) h^P​(ξ,t1)=b0,1​F​(ξ,h^​(ξ,t0)=b0,1​(−0.5​(ξ2+i​ξ))CLOSE,\hat{h}^{P}(\xi,t_{1})=b_{0,1}F(\xi,\hat{h}(\xi,t_{0})=b_{0,1}(-0.5(\xi^{2}+i\xi)),

where b0,1=Δα/Γ⁡(α+1)b_{0,1}=\Delta^{\alpha}/\Gamma(\alpha+1). The RHS of (2.15) is of the order of Δα​|ξ|2\Delta^{\alpha}|\xi|^{2}, however,

(2.16) h^​(ξ,t)=−0.5​(ξ2+i​ξ)Γ⁡(α+1)​tα​(1+o⁡(1)),\hat{h}(\xi,t)=\frac{-0.5(\xi^{2}+i\xi)}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}t^{\alpha}(1+o(1)),

uniformly in (ξ,t)(\xi,t) in the region {(ξ,t)| 0≤tα​|ξ|2<c}\{(\xi,t)\ |\ 0\leq t^{\alpha}|\xi|^{2}<c\}. See [27], where the full asymptotic expansion is calculated. We construct modifications of the Adams method changing the prediction step so that the asymptotics (2.16) is taken into account. We use the same coefficients aj,ka_{j,k} as in the fractional Adams method. Explicitly, for k=0,1,…,M−1k=0,1,\ldots,M-1, set

ak+1,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2),a0,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2)​(kα+1−(k−α)​(k+1)α),a_{k+1,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)},\ a_{0,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}(k^{\alpha+1}-(k-\alpha)(k+1)^{\alpha}),

and, in the cycle j=1,2,…,kj=1,2,\ldots,k, calculate

aj,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2)​((k−j+2)α+1+(k−j)α+1−2​(k−j+1)α+1).a_{j,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}((k-j+2)^{\alpha+1}+(k-j)^{\alpha+1}-2(k-j+1)^{\alpha+1}).

2.4.2. Modification BL in [12] a.k.a. Modification III in [22]

Introduce the scaled unknown and its leading asymptotic part

h^~​(ξ,t):=(1+|ξ|)−1​h^​(ξ,t),h^~a​s​(ξ,t):=(1+|ξ|)−1​h^a​s​(ξ,t),\tilde{\hat{h}}(\xi,t):=(1+|\xi|)^{-1}\hat{h}(\xi,t),\qquad\tilde{\hat{h}}_{as}(\xi,t):=(1+|\xi|)^{-1}\hat{h}_{as}(\xi,t),

Remark 2.1.
  1. (a)

    A pseudo-code implementation scheme for the BL Modification can be found in Appendix.

  2. (b)

    One can use asymptotic expansions of higher orders but in our numerical experiments with the two-term asymptotic expansion, the latter brings no advantages.

  3. (c)

    The accuracy of the numerical scheme can be significantly increased using the time-grid depending on ξ\xi, and non-uniform grids.

  4. (d)

    The accuracy of calculations can be increased using grids {tk}\{t_{k}\} depending on ξ\xi. If calculations of ϕ⁡(ξ,T)\phi(\xi,T) for each ξ\xi in the pricing formula are parallelized, the CPU time decreases. Non-uniform grids can be indispensable for pricing options of long maturities.

  5. (e)

    The CPU time of the BL-modification can be decreased sizably and accuracy somewhat improved using the standard prediction-correction method starting with some tk∗​(ξ)t^{*}_{k}(\xi) and larger step starting at tk∗​(ξ)t^{*}_{k}(\xi). Indeed, outside a neighborhood of 0 (which depends on ξ\xi and the parameters of the model), the solution is sufficiently regular and not small, hence, there is no advantage to use the leading term of asymptotics. We leave to the future the study of an approximately optimal choice of tk∗​(ξ)t^{*}_{k}(\xi).

  6. (f)

    In the numerical examples, we use tk∗​(ξ)=0.02t^{*}_{k}(\xi)=0.02 for all ξ\xi, and call the resulting hybrid method the BL-Adams method.

  7. (g)

    Outside a neighborhood of zero, alternative methods can be used. See [27, 60] and the bibliographies therein. These methods can be more efficient outside a small vicinity of zero than the BL-Adams method. We leave the study of improvements of our technique along this line to the future. Improvements of this kind can be very useful for option pricing and study of the ATM skew in the long run.

Remark 2.2.

BL-modification can be applied to more general kernels K⁡(t)K(t). Assume that (after the rescaling, if necessary) K⁡(t)=tα−1​(1+o⁡(1))K(t)=t^{\alpha-1}(1+o(1)) as t→0+t\to 0+. Then BL-modification is applied exactly as in the case K⁡(t)=tα−1K(t)=t^{\alpha-1}. Naturally, the coefficients of the Adams method must be recalculated for the given KK. If more than one term of the asymptotics of K⁡(t)K(t) is available, additional asymptotic terms in BL-modification can be added. Additional terms can be added if K⁡(t)=tα−1K(t)=t^{\alpha-1} as well but we found that adding one or two additional terms does not improve the performance of BL-modification. If the kernel is regularized in the vicinity of 0, e.g., K⁡(t):=K⁡(ϵ,t)=(ϵ+t)α−1​(1+o⁡(t))K(t):=K(\epsilon,t)=(\epsilon+t)^{\alpha-1}(1+o(t)), where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a small parameter, then, in the formula for the leading term of h⁡(t)h(t), one replaces tαt^{\alpha} with (ϵ+t)α(\epsilon+t)^{\alpha}.

2.4.3. Modification SQ

We use the label SQ to denote seemingly natural modification of the Adams method: due to a special form of the integrand, h^​(ξ,tk+1)\hat{h}(\xi,t_{k+1}) can be calculated explicitly solving the quadratic equation for h^​(ξ,tk+1)\hat{h}(\xi,t_{k+1}). The errors of a numerical method for the solution of an integral equation strongly depend on the regularity of the solution. In the BL modification, we solve the equation for the auxiliary function which is more regular than the initial one. In Modification SQ, the unknown function remains the same, hence, the errors in the region of small tt remain large. There are two additional disadvantages. First, the solution of the quadratic equation is more time consuming that the simple iteration method at each step of the Adams method. For the same tt-grids, the CPU time is 10-20% larger; the cumulative error of the simple iteration with 5-10 steps is smaller than the error of the Adams method (or its BL modification) itself, hence, a more accurate evaluation of h^​(ξ,tk+1)\hat{h}(\xi,t_{k+1}) brings no significant advantages. Secondly, the expression for the square root in the formula for hk+1,k+1​(ξ,t)h_{k+1,k+1}(\xi,t) may cross the cut (−∞,0](-\infty,0] as tt increases and then the pricing algorithm produces an incorrect result. Finally, in the application to evaluation of the characteristic function in the rough Heston model, we observe that the errors of the SQ modification are larger than the errors of the Adams method and the BL modification.

2.4.4. Errors of the evaluation of h⁡(ξ,τ)h(\xi,\tau)

We evaluate h⁡(ξ,τ)h(\xi,\tau) for τ≤1​M\tau\leq 1M and ξ\xi on the line {Imξ=−0.5}\{\operatorname{\rm Im}\xi=-0.5\} using the standard Adams method (Adams1 in Fig. 4-5) and the BL modification. In both cases, M=40000M=40000 is fairly large, and the results agree extremely well. Then we take a moderate M=1000M=1000 and calculate errors of the BL modification, Adams1, and SQ modification (labelled Adams2 in the figures). It is seen that the BL modification is significantly more accurate than the standard Adams method, and the SQ modification is significantly less accurate than the standard Adams method.

In Fig. 6, we show the values of ϕ⁡(τ,ξj)\phi(\tau,\xi_{j}), τ=1/52\tau=1/52, ξj=−0.5​i+yj\xi_{j}=-0.5i+y_{j}, where yjy_{j} are nodes of the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature with 200200 terms. The curves on the left (resp., right) panel are obtained using the SQ (resp., BL) modifications. Assuming that the conjecture about the asymptotics of ϕ⁡(ξ,τ)\phi(\xi,\tau) as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty is correct, for very large MM, the curve (ℝ+∋y)→ϕ⁡(−0.5​i+y,τ)({\mathbb{R}}_{+}\ni y)\to\phi(-0.5i+y,\tau) must have an (approximate) asymptote. If this is the case, the curves evaluated using the QS-modification approach the asymptote from below as M→∞M\to\infty, and the ones evaluated using the BL-modification - from above. One observes that

  1. (a)

    the errors of the former are larger than the ones of the latter;

  2. (b)

    if the SQ modification is used, Re⁡ϕ⁡(−0.5​i+y,τ)→−∞\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(-0.5i+y,\tau)\to-\infty as y→+∞y\to+\infty significantly faster than the correct Re⁡ϕ⁡(−0.5​i+y,τ)\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(-0.5i+y,\tau) which we expect to be closer to the asymptote. Hence, if MM is not very large, the Gauss-Laguerre quadratures with 100 nodes and more will produce seemingly rapidly converging sequence of prices; but the errors - small but not very small - remain of the same order of magnitude;

  3. (c)

    if the BL modification is used and MM is insufficiently large, then the sequence Re⁡ϕ⁡(−0.5​i+yj,τ)\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(-0.5i+y_{j},\tau) may start to increase, hence, the errors in prices increase and become quite substantial as NN increases. This explains the calibration/pricing errors in the example shown on [12, Fig. 7], where the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature with 200 nodes and BL-modification with M=1000M=1000 are used.

2.5. Markovian approximation of rough volatility

The rough Heston model is characterized by a fractional integral in the dynamics of the volatility process. The key idea of the Markovian approximation is to replace the non-Markovian fractional process with a high-dimensional Markovian process that has similar dynamics [7]. One observes that the fractional kernel of the rough Heston model K⁡(t)=cα​tα−1K(t)=c_{\alpha}t^{\alpha-1} is a complete monotone function, hence, by Bernstein’s theorem, can be represented as an integral of exponential functions:

K⁡(t)=∫0∞e−y​t​μ​(𝑑y),K(t)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-yt}\mu(dy),

where μ⁡(d​y)\mu(dy) is a positive measure. One approximates μ⁡(d​y)\mu(dy) by a weighted sum of atoms, thereby approximating K⁡(t)K(t) by a finite weighted sum of exponentials:

(2.22) Kn​(t)=∑j=1ncj​e−yj​t.K^{n}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}e^{-y_{j}t}.

The weights cic_{i} and exponents yiy_{i} are chosen in order to match the original kernel K⁡(t)K(t) as closely as possible. This transforms the original non-Markovian rough Heston model into a higher-dimensional, but Markovian, system which is more amenable to standard pricing techniques. Following [7, §1], we can define the approximation (Sn,Vn)(S^{n},V^{n}) of (S,V)(S,V) as follows

(2.23) d​Stn\displaystyle dS^{n}_{t} =Stn​Vtn​d​Bt,S0n=S0,\displaystyle=S^{n}_{t}\sqrt{V^{n}_{t}}dB_{t},\qquad S^{n}_{0}=S_{0},
(2.24) Vtn\displaystyle V^{n}_{t} =V0+∫0tKn​(t−s)​γ​(θ−Vsn)​𝑑s+∫0tKn​(t−s)​γ​ν​Vsn​d​Ws.\displaystyle=V_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}K^{n}(t-s)\,\gamma(\theta-V^{n}_{s})\,ds+\int_{0}^{t}K^{n}(t-s)\gamma\nu\sqrt{V^{n}_{s}}\,dW_{s}.

In [50] it was shown that VnV^{n} solves an nn-dimensional SDE. In [7], different schemes for the approximations KnK^{n} are compared, including those proposed in earlier studies, e.g. in [50], [2], [6]. Of these, the scheme called “BL2” was shown in [7] to be the fastest and most accurate. This rule minimizes the L2L^{2} error between KNK^{N} and KK, while penalizing large nodes. The corresponding algorithm can be found in Appendix F of [7].

The SINH-CB method can be applied in this setting to price not only European options, but barrier and lookback options as well, after the approximation by a regime-switching Lévy model or time discretization, and using the schemes in [24, 23, 21, 25].

3. Flat iFT, SINH-acceleration and Conformal Bootstrap principle

3.1. Flat iFT and simplified trapezoid rule

In popular models, the (conditional) characteristic function admits analytic continuation to a strip around the real axis. This implies that the following scheme (standard from the viewpoint of Analysis) suggested in [13, 14, 15] is more efficient than the scheme in [47] based on the Lévy inversion formula. Let the riskless rate r≥0r\geq 0 be constant, and let ST=S0​eXTS_{T}=S_{0}e^{X_{T}} be the price of the underlying non-dividend paying asset (or index) at time TT. Let Φ⁡(ξ,T)=𝔼⁡[ei​ξ​XT]\Phi(\xi,T)={\mathbb{E}}[e^{i\xi X_{T}}] be the characteristic function of XTX_{T} under a no-arbitrage measure ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} chosen for pricing (the expectation is conditioned on the spot values of additional factors as in SV models). Then Φ⁡(0,T)=1\Phi(0,T)=1, and if 𝔼ℚ​[eXT]<∞{\mathbb{E}}^{\mathbb{Q}}[e^{X_{T}}]<\infty, Φ⁡(−i,T)=er​T\Phi(-i,T)=e^{rT}. Assume that there exist μ−​(T)<−1<0<μ+​(T)\mu_{-}(T)<-1<0<\mu_{+}(T) s.t. for β∈(−μ+​(T),−μ−​(T))\beta\in(-\mu_{+}(T),-\mu_{-}(T)), the exponential moments 𝔼ℚ​[eβ​XT]{\mathbb{E}}^{\mathbb{Q}}[e^{\beta X_{T}}] are finite. Equivalently, Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) admits analytic continuation to a strip S(μ−​(T),μ+​(T)):={ξ|Im⁡ξ∈(μ−​(T),μ+​(T))}S_{(\mu_{-}(T),\mu_{+}(T))}:=\{\xi\ |\ \operatorname{\rm Im}\xi\in(\mu_{-}(T),\mu_{+}(T))\}. Then the price of the call option with strike KK and maturity TT can be calculated as follows. The payoff function G⁡(S0,K,x)=(S0​ex−K)+G(S_{0},K,x)=(S_{0}e^{x}-K)_{+} admits a representation

(3.1) G⁡(S0,K,x)=12​π​∫Im⁡ξ=ω1ei​x​ξ​G^​(S0,K,ξ)​𝑑ξ,G(S_{0},K;x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\operatorname{\rm Im}\xi=\omega_{1}}e^{ix\xi}{\hat{G}}(S_{0},K;\xi)d\xi,

where ω1∈(μ−​(T),−1)\omega_{1}\in(\mu_{-}(T),-1) is arbitrary, and G^(S0,K;ξ)=−Kei​ξ​ln⁡(S0/K)/(ξ(ξ+i)){\hat{G}}(S_{0},K;\xi)=-Ke^{i\xi\ln(S_{0}/K)}/(\xi(\xi+i)) is the Fourier transform of G⁡(S0,K,x)G(S_{0},K;x) w.r.t. xx. We substitute the integral representation (3.1) of G⁡(S0,K,XT)G(S_{0},K;X_{T}) into the pricing formula V⁡(S0,K,T)=e−r​T​𝔼​[(S0​eXT−K)+]V(S_{0},K;T)=e^{-rT}{\mathbb{E}}[(S_{0}e^{X_{T}}-K)_{+}], and change the order of integration and summation (the use of the Fubini theorem can be justified in all popular models). The result is

(3.2) V(S0,K;T)=−K​e−r​TπRe∫Im⁡ξ=ω1ei​ξ​ln⁡(S0/K)​Φ​(T,ξ)ξ⁡(ξ+i)dξ.V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{Ke^{-rT}}{\pi}\operatorname{\rm Re}\int_{\operatorname{\rm Im}\xi=\omega_{1}}\frac{e^{i\xi\ln(S_{0}/K)}\Phi(T,\xi)}{\xi(\xi+i)}d\xi.

Similarly, the price of the put is given by the RHS of (3.2) with arbitrary ω1∈(0,μ+​(T))\omega_{1}\in(0,\mu_{+}(T)) (repeat the proof for the call starting with G⁡(x)=(K−S0​ex)+G(x)=(K-S_{0}e^{x})_{+} or use the put-call parity on the LHS of (3.2) and the residue theorem on the RHS). The price of the covered call is given by the RHS of (3.2) with ω1∈(−1,0)\omega_{1}\in(-1,0). Since Φ⁡(ξ,T)¯=Φ⁡(−ξ¯,T)\overline{\Phi(\xi,T)}=\Phi(-\bar{\xi},T) and G^​(ξ)¯=G^​(−ξ¯)\overline{{\hat{G}}(\xi)}={\hat{G}}(-\bar{\xi}), an equivalent form of (3.2) is

(3.3) V(S0,K;T)=−K​e−r​TπRe∫Im⁡ξ=ω1ei​ξ​ln⁡(S0/K)​Φ​(ξ,T)ξ⁡(ξ+i)dξ.V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{Ke^{-rT}}{\pi}\operatorname{\rm Re}\int_{\operatorname{\rm Im}\xi=\omega_{1}}\frac{e^{i\xi\ln(S_{0}/K)}\Phi(\xi,T)}{\xi(\xi+i)}d\xi.

After truncation, the integral on the RHS of (3.2) (or (3.3)) can be calculated using either trapezoid rule or Simpson rule.

However, since the integrand on the RHS of (3.2) is analytic in a strip S(λ−,λ+)S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})} around the line of integration (λ−=μ−​(T),λ+=−1\lambda_{-}=\mu_{-}(T),\lambda_{+}=-1 in the case of calls, λ−=−1,λ+=0\lambda_{-}=-1,\lambda_{+}=0 in the case of the covered call, and λ−=0,λ+=μ+​(T)\lambda_{-}=0,\lambda_{+}=\mu_{+}(T) in the case of puts), it is significantly more efficient to use the infinite trapezoid rule and then truncate the sum. The reason is an exponential decay of the discretization error of the infinite trapezoid rule as the function of ζ\zeta, where ζ\zeta is the step. In Mathematical Finance, Lee [52] and Feng and Linetsky [38] were the first to use this important property of the infinite trapezoid rule; the truncation of the sum results in the simplified trapezoid rule. As it is stated in the review paper [63], the excellent properties of the simplified trapezoid rule had been noticed since Poisson but rigorously proved in the middle of the last century only. Let H1​(S(λ−,λ+))H^{1}(S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})}) denote the space of functions analytic in the strip S(λ−,λ+)S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})} such that

∫λ−λ+|f⁡(η+i​ω)|​𝑑ω→0as⁡(ℝ∋)​η→±∞\int_{\lambda_{-}}^{\lambda_{+}}|f(\eta+i\omega)|d\omega\to 0\quad{\rm as}\ ({\mathbb{R}}\ni)\eta\to\pm\infty

and the following analog of the Hardy norm is finite:

(3.4) ‖f‖S(λ−,λ+):=limω↑λ+∫ℝ|f⁡(η+i​ω)|​𝑑η+limω↓λ−∫ℝ|f⁡(η+i​ω)|​𝑑η<∞.||f||_{S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})}}:=\lim_{\omega\uparrow\lambda_{+}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|f(\eta+i\omega)|d\eta+\lim_{\omega\downarrow\lambda_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|f(\eta+i\omega)|d\eta<\infty.

Fix ω1∈(λ−,λ+)\omega_{1}\in(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+}), and denote d⁡(ω1)=min⁡{ω1−λ−,λ+−ω1}d(\omega_{1})=\min\{\omega_{1}-\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+}-\omega_{1}\}. For ζ>0\zeta>0, construct a grid ξ=i​ω1+ζ​ℤ\xi=i\omega_{1}+\zeta{\mathbb{Z}}, and denote by Edisc​(ζ,∞)E_{\rm disc}(\zeta,\infty) the error of the infinite trapezoid rule

∫Im⁡ξ=ωf⁡(ξ)​𝑑ξ≈ζ​∑j∈ℤf⁡(ξj).\int_{\operatorname{\rm Im}\xi=\omega}f(\xi)d\xi\approx\zeta\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{Z}}}f(\xi_{j}).

The following bound is proved in [62] using the heavy machinery of the sinc-functions (a simple proof can be found in [53], and several other elementary bounds and proofs in [63]):

(3.5) |Edisc​(ζ,∞)|≤e−2πd(ω1)/ζ1−e−2πd(ω1)/ζ​‖f‖S(λ−,λ+).\left|E_{\rm disc}(\zeta,\infty)\right|\leq\frac{e^{-2\pi d(\omega_{1})/\zeta}}{1-e^{-2\pi d(\omega_{1})/\zeta}}||f||_{S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})}}.

Let the error tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon>0 for the discretization error be small, and let |μ±||\mu_{\pm}| be not too large. Then we choose ω1=(λ−+λ+)/2\omega_{1}=(\lambda_{-}+\lambda_{+})/2, set d⁡(ω1)=kd​(λ+−λ−)/2d(\omega_{1})=k_{d}(\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-})/2, where kd<1k_{d}<1 is close to 1, e.g., kd=0.95k_{d}=0.95, and use the following approximate recommendation:

(3.6) ζ=2​d​(ω1)/ln⁡(100/ϵ).\zeta=2d(\omega_{1})/\ln(100/\epsilon).

If the strip of analyticity is very wide, we choose a substrip around the line of integration with moderately large |λ±||\lambda_{\pm}| and apply the prescription above.

Once ζ\zeta is chosen and the sum is truncated, we have the pricing formula. In the case of (3.2),

(3.7) V(S0,K;T)=−K​e−r​T​ζ2​π∑|j|≤Nei​ξj​ln⁡(S0/K)​Φ​(ξj,T)ξj​(ξj+i),V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{Ke^{-rT}\zeta}{2\pi}\sum_{|j|\leq N}\frac{e^{i\xi_{j}\ln(S_{0}/K)}\Phi(\xi_{j},T)}{\xi_{j}(\xi_{j}+i)},

where ξj=i​ω1+j​ζ\xi_{j}=i\omega_{1}+j\zeta. The number of terms can be decreased almost two-fold: similarly to (3.3),

(3.8) V(S0,K;T)=−K​e−r​T​ζπRe∑0≤j≤N(1−δj​0/2)ei​ξj​ln⁡(S0/K)​Φ​(ξj,T)ξj​(ξj+i),V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{Ke^{-rT}\zeta}{\pi}\operatorname{\rm Re}\sum_{0\leq j\leq N}(1-\delta_{j0}/2)\frac{e^{i\xi_{j}\ln(S_{0}/K)}\Phi(\xi_{j},T)}{\xi_{j}(\xi_{j}+i)},

where δj​k\delta_{jk} is the Kronecker symbol. We call this method Flat iFT (flat inverse Fourier transform) method. To choose NN so that the truncation error is sufficiently small, it is necessary to know the rate of decay of Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty along the contour of integration. Let Φ⁡(ξ,T)=exp⁡[ϕ⁡(ξ,T)]\Phi(\xi,T)=\exp[\phi(\xi,T)], and let an upper bound for Re⁡ϕ⁡(ξ,T)\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(\xi,T) be known:

(3.9) Re⁡ϕ⁡(ξ,T)<−g⁡(|ξ|,T),\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(\xi,T)<-g(|\xi|,T),

where g⁡(|ξ|,T)g(|\xi|,T) is a monotonically increasing function of |ξ||\xi|. Then the truncation of the series at |ξ|=Λ0|\xi|=\Lambda_{0} introduces the error of the order of e−g⁡(Λ0,T)/Λ0e^{-g(\Lambda_{0},T)}/\Lambda_{0}. If an analytic formula for ϕ⁡(ξ,T)=ln⁡Φ⁡(ξ,T)\phi(\xi,T)=\ln\Phi(\xi,T) is available, then an efficient bound (3.9) can be derived. See [53, 54]. In the case of the rough Heston model, an analytic formula is not available. In Sect. 3.3, we use an informally proved asymptotic formula (see Sect. 2.2) to formulate a prescription for the choice of Λ0\Lambda_{0}. In the case of Flat iFT, the asymptotic formula and the prescription should be used with ω=0\omega=0. After Λ0\Lambda_{0} is calculated, we set N=ceil​Λ0/ζN=\mathrm{ceil}\,\Lambda_{0}/\zeta.

3.2. SINH-acceleration

The SINH-acceleration is applicable if the (conditional on the spot value of the underlying and additional factors, as in the case of SV models) characteristic function Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) of XTX_{T} admits analytic continuation to the union of a strip S(a,b):={ξ|Im⁡ξ∈(a,b)}S_{(a,b)}:=\{\xi\ |\ \operatorname{\rm Im}\xi\in(a,b)\}, where a≤−1<0≤ba\leq-1<0\leq b, and a cone around −0.5​i+ℝ-0.5i+{\mathbb{R}}. For the Heston model and rough Heston model, conditions on the parameters of the model and TT which guarantee analyticity of Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) in the strip S[−1,0]S_{[-1,0]} are known [52, 53, 45]. If Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) admits analytic continuation to S[−1,0]S_{[-1,0]}, then the existence of a cone of analyticity around −0.5​i+ℝ-0.5i+{\mathbb{R}} is proved in [53] for the Heston model, and in [54] for wide classes of SV models and models with stochastic interest rates. We surmise that the (conditional) characteristic function in the rough Heston model enjoys the same property but we were unable to prove this fact. In Sect. 3.4, we explain how the CB principle can be used to heuristically establish this property for any set of the parameters of the rough Heston model.

In the Heston model and rough Heston model, the integral (3.2) can be calculated sufficiently accurately for applications using the Flat iFT method with 200-400 terms if the time to maturity is not too short. The errors depend on the choice of the line of integration. In the real-analytic interpretation [28], choices of different lines of integration are choices of different dampening factors. In Complex Analysis, one observes that the Fourier transform f^{\hat{f}} of a sufficiently regular function ff is an analytic function in a wide region 𝒰0{\mathcal{U}}_{0} of the complex plane and meromorphic function in a wider region 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}. We choose 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} so that f^​(ξ)→0{\hat{f}}(\xi)\to 0 sufficiently fast as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty remaining in 𝒰{\mathcal{U}}. The inverse Fourier transform can be calculated deforming the line of integration into any sufficiently regular curve in 𝒰0{\mathcal{U}}_{0}; crossing poles, one can reduce to the integral over any sufficiently regular curve in 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} (plus residues at the poles crossed in the process of deformation).

In all popular models bar stable Lévy models different from BM, Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) admits analytic continuation to a region of the form 𝒰⁡(γ−,γ+,μ+,μ−):=i⁡(μ+,μ−)+(𝒞γ−,γ+∪(−𝒞−γ+,γ−)∪{0}){\mathcal{U}}(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+};\mu_{+},\mu_{-}):=i(\mu_{+},\mu_{-})+({\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}}\cup(-{\mathcal{C}}_{-\gamma_{+},\gamma_{-}})\cup\{0\}), where μ−<−1<0<μ+\mu_{-}<-1<0<\mu_{+}, 𝒞γ−,γ+:={ξ∈ℂ|arg​ξ∈(γ−,γ+)}{\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}}:=\{\xi\in{\mathbb{C}}\ |\mathrm{arg}\,\xi\in(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+})\}. In the case of Lévy models, 𝒰⁡(γ−,γ+,μ+,μ−){\mathcal{U}}(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+};\mu_{+},\mu_{-}) is independent of TT. In the Heston model and other SV models, the domain of analyticity depends on TT. In the case of the Heston model, under additional restriction on the parameters, it is proved in [58] that Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) is analytic in 𝒰=ℂ∖i((−∞,μ−(T)]∪[μ+(T),+∞)){\mathcal{U}}={\mathbb{C}}\setminus i((-\infty,\mu_{-}(T)]\cup[\mu_{+}(T),+\infty)), where μ−​(T)<−1<0<μ+​(T)\mu_{-}(T)<-1<0<\mu_{+}(T); in [53], this fact is proved for jump-diffusion generalizations of the Heston model, with more than one factor driving the dynamics of the volatility process, and algebraic equations for μ−​(T)\mu_{-}(T) and μ+​(T)\mu_{+}(T) were derived. For wide classes of affine jump-diffusion processes, it is proved in [54] that Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) is an analytic function on the union 𝒰0​(μ−​(T),μ+​(T),γ−,γ+){\mathcal{U}}_{0}(\mu_{-}(T),\mu_{+}(T),\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}) of a strip S(μ−​(T),μ+​(T))S_{(\mu_{-}(T),\mu_{+}(T))}, where μ−​(T)<−1<0<μ+​(T)\mu_{-}(T)<-1<0<\mu_{+}(T), and a cone 𝒞γ−,γ+:={ξ=ρ​ei​φ|φ∈(γ−,γ+)∨φ∈(π−γ−,π−γ+)}{\mathcal{C}}_{\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}}:=\{\xi=\rho e^{i\varphi}\ |\ \varphi\in(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+})\vee\varphi\in(\pi-\gamma_{-},\pi-\gamma_{+})\}, where γ−∈(−π/2,0),γ+∈(0,π/2)\gamma_{-}\in(-\pi/2,0),\gamma_{+}\in(0,\pi/2) (typically, γ±=±π/4\gamma_{\pm}=\pm\pi/4; in the case of the Heston model, γ±=±π/2\gamma_{\pm}=\pm\pi/2), and decays as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty remaining in the cone. Once the existence of such a strip and cone is established, we choose a deformation of the contour of integration into a contour ℒω1,b,ω:=χω1,b,ω​(ℝ){\mathcal{L}}_{\omega_{1},b,\omega}:=\chi_{\omega_{1},b,\omega}({\mathbb{R}}), where ω1∈ℝ\omega_{1}\in{\mathbb{R}}, b>0b>0, ω∈(γ−,γ+)\omega\in(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+}), and the conformal map χω1,b,ω\chi_{\omega_{1},b,\omega} (sinh-deformation) is defined by

(3.10) χω1,b,ω​(y)=i​ω1+b​sinh⁡(i​ω+y).\chi_{\omega_{1},b,\omega}(y)=i\omega_{1}+b\sinh(i\omega+y).

The parameters of the deformation are chosen so that in the process of deformation, the contour remains in 𝒰⁡(γ−,γ+,μ+,μ−){\mathcal{U}}(\gamma_{-},\gamma_{+};\mu_{+},\mu_{-}), the oscillating factor becomes a fast decreasing one and the poles at ξ=0,−i\xi=0,-i are not crossed. The deformation being made, we change the variable ξ=ξ⁡(y)=χω1,b,ω​(y)\xi=\xi(y)=\chi_{\omega_{1},b,\omega}(y) in (3.2)

(3.11) V(S0,K;T)=−b​K​e−r​T2​π∫ℝei​ξ​(y)​ln⁡(S0/K)​Φ​(ξ⁡(y),T)ξ​(y)​(ξ​(y)+i)cosh(iω+y)dy,V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{bKe^{-rT}}{2\pi}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{e^{i\xi(y)\ln(S_{0}/K)}\Phi(\xi(y),T)}{\xi(y)(\xi(y)+i)}\cosh(i\omega+y)dy,

and apply the simplified trapezoid rule:

(3.12) V(S0,K;T)=−b​ζ​K​e−r​TπRe∑j=0Nei​ξ​(j​ζ)​ln⁡(S0/K)g(jζ,T)(1−δ0​j/2),V(S_{0},K;T)=-\frac{b\zeta Ke^{-rT}}{\pi}\operatorname{\rm Re}\sum_{j=0}^{N}e^{i\xi(j\zeta)\ln(S_{0}/K)}g(j\zeta,T)(1-\delta_{0j}/2),

where g⁡(y,T)=Φ⁡(ξ⁡(y),T)ξ​(y)​(ξ​(y)+i)​cosh⁡(i​ω+y)g(y,T)=\frac{\Phi(\xi(y),T)}{\xi(y)(\xi(y)+i)}\cosh(i\omega+y).

The change of variables ξ=χω1,b,ω​(y)\xi=\chi_{\omega_{1},b,\omega}(y) makes the integrand a fast decaying one in a strip of the form S(−d,d)S_{(-d,d)}, hence, the error of the truncation of the infinite sum is easy to control. Fig.7 illustrates the sinh-acceleration. In essentially all cases we tried, an absolute error tolerance of the order of E−09E-09 can be satisfied with 20-60 terms of the simplified trapezoid rule.

Explicit recommendations for the choice of the parameters of the deformation ω1,b,ω\omega_{1},b,\omega and parameters ζ,N\zeta,N of the simplified trapezoid rule are derived in [18]. We add several useful details for the case of the rough Heston model.

  1. I.

    Find μ±​(T)\mu_{\pm}(T) and γ±\gamma_{\pm}.

  2. II.

    Calculate zTz_{T} using (3.13) below. If zT≤0z_{T}\leq 0, use ω≤0\omega\leq 0 and calculate the price of either the call or covered call; otherwise, use ω≥0\omega\geq 0 and calculate the price of either the put or covered call.

  3. III.
    1. (a)

      If the call is priced, set λ−=μ−​(T),λ+=−1\lambda_{-}=\mu_{-}(T),\lambda_{+}=-1, ω=γ−/2\omega=\gamma_{-}/2, d0=−ωd_{0}=-\omega.

    2. (b)

      If the put is priced, set λ−=0,λ+=μ+​(T)\lambda_{-}=0,\lambda_{+}=\mu_{+}(T), ω=γ+/2\omega=\gamma_{+}/2, d0=ωd_{0}=\omega.

    3. (c)

      If the covered call is priced, set λ−=−1,λ+=0\lambda_{-}=-1,\lambda_{+}=0. If S0<KS_{0}<K, set ω=γ−​(T)/2\omega=\gamma_{-}(T)/2, d0=−ωd_{0}=-\omega. If S0>KS_{0}>K, set ω=γ+​(T)/2\omega=\gamma_{+}(T)/2, d0=ωd_{0}=\omega.

    4. (d)

      For ATM options, it is optimal to set ω=(γ−+γ+)/2\omega=(\gamma_{-}+\gamma_{+})/2, d0=(γ+−γ−)/2d_{0}=(\gamma_{+}-\gamma_{-})/2.

  4. IV.

    Choose kd<1k_{d}<1 close to 1, e.g., kd=0.9k_{d}=0.9, and set d=kd​d0d=k_{d}d_{0}, ζ=2​π​d/ln⁡(100/ϵ)\zeta=2\pi d/\ln(100/\epsilon),

    b=λ+−λ−sin⁡(ω+d)−sin⁡(ω−d),ω1=λ−​sin⁡(ω+d)−λ+​sin⁡(ω−d)sin⁡(ω+d)−sin⁡(ω−d).b=\frac{\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}}{\sin(\omega+d)-\sin(\omega-d)},\ \omega_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{-}\sin(\omega+d)-\lambda_{+}\sin(\omega-d)}{\sin(\omega+d)-\sin(\omega-d)}.
  5. V.

    As in the case of Flat iFT, to choose NN so that the truncation error is sufficiently small, it is necessary to know the rate of decay of Φ⁡(ξ,T)\Phi(\xi,T) as ξ→∞\xi\to\infty along the contour of integration. Let Φ⁡(ξ,T)=exp⁡[ϕ⁡(ξ,T)]\Phi(\xi,T)=\exp[\phi(\xi,T)], and let an upper bound (3.9) for Re⁡ϕ⁡(ξ,T)\operatorname{\rm Re}\phi(\xi,T) be known. In the yy-coordinate, the series decays as (K​ζ​b/π)​e−g⁡(|ξ⁡(yj)|,T)/|ξ⁡(yj)|(K\zeta b/\pi)e^{-g(|\xi(y_{j})|,T)}/|\xi(y_{j})|. Since |ξ⁡(y)||\xi(y)| increases as an exponential function of yy as y→±∞y\to\pm\infty, the truncation error is smaller than the last term of the truncated sum if g⁡(|ξ⁡(yj)|,T)g(|\xi(y_{j})|,T) is large. We find the positive solution Λ0\Lambda_{0} of the equation e−g⁡(Λ0,T)/Λ0=b​π​ϵ/(K​ζ)e^{-g(\Lambda_{0},T)}/\Lambda_{0}=b\pi\epsilon/(K\zeta), and set Λ=ln⁡(2​Λ0/(K​b))\Lambda=\ln(2\Lambda_{0}/(Kb)), N=ceil​Λ/ζN=\mathrm{ceil}\,\Lambda/\zeta.

Remark 3.1.

The recommendation ζ=2​π​d/ln⁡(100/ϵ)\zeta=2\pi d/\ln(100/\epsilon) presumes that ‖f‖S(λ−,λ+)||f||_{S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})}}, the analogue (3.4) of the Hardy norm of the integrand, is bounded by 100. A safer alternative which we used in several publications is to use the approximation ||f||S(λ−,λ+)≈|f(i(ω+d))|+|f(i(ω−d)))|||f||_{S_{(\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+})}}\approx|f(i(\omega+d))|+|f(i(\omega-d)))|.

3.3. Ad-hoc bound for ϕ\phi and choice of NN in the rough Heston model

To choose Λ:=N​ζ\Lambda:=N\zeta, we use (2.13)-(2.14). The leading term of asymptotics of the expression under the exponential sign in the pricing formula is

(−c∞​(T)+i​ln⁡(S0/K))​ξ=i​zT​ξ−Re⁡c∞​ξ,(-c_{\infty}(T)+i\ln(S_{0}/K))\xi=iz_{T}\xi-\operatorname{\rm Re}c_{\infty}\xi,

where
